newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil officials under guard after death threats.
newsitem.headline: Brazil officials under guard after death threats.

text.p: Two senior Brazilian government officials have been placed under police guard after receiving death threats for their efforts to change Latin America's largest country, officials said on Monday.
A farmer angry at government attempts to settle landless peasants threatened to kill Agrarian Reform Minister Raul Jungmann, a spokeswoman for the minister said.

And a spokesman for the Administration Ministry said its executive secretary, Claudia Costin, had been placed under 24-hour protection because of death threats that followed a plan to slash 200,000 federal jobs.
Brazil, though rife with street violence and crime, rarely experiences such extreme reactions to official decisions.

"The Brazilian civil service system used to be based on privilege and favour-trading. For the first time, the government is trying to end this tradition. Perhaps that's why we're seeing such violent reactions," Costin's spokesman said.

He said the executive secretary was threatened two days after an Oct. 11 announcement of wide-ranging plans to cut spending and raise revenue, designed to save up to $6.5 billion next year and cut 200,000 federal posts.
"There is a clear connection (between the job cuts and the threats)," he said.
The threats stopped after police announced last Wednesday they would be tracing all calls to Costin.
Jungmann was first threatened last week by an armed landowner who stormed into his ministry, his spokeswoman said.
She could not immediately confirm reports that the gunman demanded $17 million in compensation for land that was "disappropriated" under Brasilia's agrarian reform programme.

Brazil has one of the world's least balanced distributions of income and land. The 307 largest landowners possess four percent of Brazil while, on the other side, the militant Landless Movement claims to represent up to five million landless families.
The government of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has pledged to settle 280,000 families by the end of his mandate in just over two years.
